suggestions.assertion: Project background and purpose are not restated; the Daily covers the session delta only
suggestions.reason: This assertion is not discriminating as written. The output passes it (no background prose) while still committing the failure mode the assertion is presumably aimed at: ~40% of the document is out-of-session repo investigation (SESSION_SECRET fallback, missing vitest, stale ARCHITECTURE.md, package.json script inventory, git object hashes) that no one asked for and that drives the 21,085-character size. Consider an assertion like 'every item in the handoff traces to something that happened in the session; incidental repo findings are excluded or confined to a single short section.'

suggestions.assertion: Daily Handoff is at most 12,000 characters
suggestions.reason: This is currently the only assertion pushing back on verbosity, and it is doing all the work - it is the sole failure across 18 assertions while the content assertions all pass comfortably. Since a skill can pass 17/18 while producing something the user must still spend 10 minutes reading, consider a second structural constraint (e.g. section count cap, or 'no fact appears in more than two sections'). The cookie decision, the legacy freeze, the 10 req/s limit and the SPEC move are each restated in 3-4 different sections here.

suggestions.assertion: No factual claim is stated confidently without support
suggestions.reason: Hard to grade as a binary - I found one unhedged unverified claim ('session.ts ... compiles as a standalone module') in an otherwise scrupulously hedged document, and had to make a judgement call to pass it. Consider narrowing it to the specific facts that matter and are hallucination-prone (staging DB state, AUTH-214 existence, test execution, TTL ownership), which are individually checkable.

No assertion checks for invented facts. This run produced none - every repo-derived detail I spot-checked (jose@5.9.6, COOKIE_NAME, TTL_SECONDS, migration columns, HEAD sha, no-upstream) was accurate - but a weaker skill could fabricate a commit sha or a dependency version and pass all 18 assertions. A 'no fabricated file paths, commands, versions or identifiers' assertion would catch that.

eval_feedback.overall: The assertions cover fact-fidelity thoroughly and the skill scores well on them (17/18). The one failure is size: 21,085 characters against a 12,000 cap, 5.85x the 3,605-character transcript it replaces. That single assertion is carrying the entire signal about conciseness, and the content assertions are all satisfiable by an over-long document, so the eval currently rewards completeness far more than it penalises bloat.
